"However, in his submissions he raised an objection. Which in his opinion, if the taxing master would have considered, would probably have reached a different decision. In light of Article 159 (2) (d) that states that “justice will be done without undue regard to procedural technicalities” I will consider the response in the submissions as objections raised. With paragraph 22 above in mind, does invoking natural justice and Fair hearing under Article 50 and 47 of the constitution ousters the provision of paragraph 11? I think not. Although the Applicant has framed the application as one alleging an error apparent on the face of the record and denial of a fair hearing, the effect of the application seeks to impeach and set aside the decision of the taxing officer. Such a challenge fall within the ambit of Paragraph 11 of the Advocates (Remuneration) Order. And thus, the issues of natural justice and fair hearing as raised can be well articulated in the bounds of paragraph 11 of the advocates Renumeration order." [chunk_id: Kariithi v GN Thiongo Associates (Miscellaneous Application E262of2025) 2026KEHC11082(KLR) (22July2026) (Ruling)__s2__c20]

According to the legal principles cited, a court will not normally interfere with the exercise of discretion by the taxing officer unless the taxing officer erred in principle in assessing the costs [chunk_id: Johnson Kibunja Njoka  another v Joseph Njuguna  2 others 2017KEHC6481(KLR)__s2__c14]. For the determination of the subject matter value for instruction fees, it is wholly dependent on the stage at which the fees are being taxed. Before judgment, the pleadings form the basis for determining the subject value. Once judgment has been entered, the judgment determines conclusively the value of the subject matter as a claim, regardless of how it was pleaded [chunk_id: Kamau  another v Ali  another (Environment and Land Miscellaneous Case 150of2024) 2026KEELC1365(KLR) (26February2026)__s2__c2, chunk_id: Njeri v Mathenge (Civil Appeal 5of2017) 2022KEHC14977(KLR) (2November2022) (Ruling)__s2__c3, chunk_id: Gikaria ta Anthony Gikaria  Company Advocates v Samchi Telecommunications Limited (Environment and Land Miscellaneous Case E008of2025) 2025KEELC18295(KLR) (13November2025) (Ruling)__s2__c23].

faithfulness_reasoning: The answer accurately reflects the cited principles: interference is only where the taxing officer erred in principle (with quantum usually left to the taxing officer except in exceptional cases), and subject matter value for instruction fees depends on the stage of taxation—pleadings before judgment and the judgment after judgment.

In such cases, the court has discretion to deal with the matter if the justice of the case so requires, and the appropriate remedy is to remit the matter for fresh taxation before a different taxing officer [chunk_id: Mwangi ta Raydon Mwangi  Associates Advocates v Njenga (Miscellaneous Application E025of2024) 2026KEHC13078(KLR) (13August2026) (Ruling)__s3__c12].

expected_value: The court must consider that an extension of time is an equitable remedy rather than a right, that the applicant bears the burden of laying a satisfactory basis for the delay, and that it must assess whether the respondents will suffer prejudice if the extension is granted.
answer:
According to the Supreme Court's guidelines in Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR, the court must consider the following factors when exercising its discretion to grant an extension of time:

1. Extension of time is not a right of a party. It is an equitable remedy that is only available to a deserving party at the discretion of the court [chunk_id: Jiangxi Transportation Engineering Group Ltd v Karweru Co Advocates (Miscellaneous Application E011of2022) 2024KEELRC1873(KLR) (19July2024) (Ruling)__s2__c3, Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR].

2. A party who seeks for extension of time has the burden of laying a basis to the satisfaction of the court [chunk_id: Jiangxi Transportation Engineering Group Ltd v Karweru Co Advocates (Miscellaneous Application E011of2022) 2024KEELRC1873(KLR) (19July2024) (Ruling)__s2__c3, Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR].

3. Whether the court should exercise the discretion to extend time, is a consideration to be made on a case to case basis [chunk_id: Jiangxi Transportation Engineering Group Ltd v Karweru Co Advocates (Miscellaneous Application E011of2022) 2024KEELRC1873(KLR) (19July2024) (Ruling)__s2__c3, Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR].

4. Whether there is a reasonable reason for the delay. The delay should be explained to the satisfaction of the court [chunk_id: Jiangxi Transportation Engineering Group Ltd v Karweru Co Advocates (Miscellaneous Application E011of2022) 2024KEELRC1873(KLR) (19July2024) (Ruling)__s2__c3, Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR].

5. Whether there will be any prejudice suffered by the respondents if the extension is granted [chunk_id: Jiangxi Transportation Engineering Group Ltd v Karweru Co Advocates (Miscellaneous Application E011of2022) 2024KEELRC1873(KLR) (19July2024) (Ruling)__s2__c3, Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR].

6. Whether the application has been brought without undue delay [chunk_id: Jiangxi Transportation Engineering Group Ltd v Karweru Co Advocates (Miscellaneous Application E011of2022) 2024KEELRC1873(KLR) (19July2024) (Ruling)__s2__c3, Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR].

7. Whether in certain cases, like election petitions, public interest should be a consideration for extending time [chunk_id: Jiangxi Transportation Engineering Group Ltd v Karweru Co Advocates (Miscellaneous Application E011of2022) 2024KEELRC1873(KLR) (19July2024) (Ruling)__s2__c3, Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR].
correctness_reasoning: It correctly states that extension of time is an equitable remedy, that the applicant bears the burden of justifying the delay, and that the court must consider potential prejudice to the respondents.
faithfulness_reasoning: The answer accurately reproduces the Supreme Court factors stated in the provided context, including that extension of time is an equitable remedy, the applicant bears the burden of justification, and prejudice to the respondent must be considered.
